idiom_name: event queue + handler table + hot state stream (replay latest state)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define events and states as closed or union types with one case per interaction and per screen condition; give the component one handler per event type, an ordered event queue, a reducer that computes the next state from (current state, event) without mutating the state object, and a hot state stream that keeps the latest state and replays it to new subscribers. Register observers for events, transitions and errors so logging and analytics need no feature code, keep one component per feature, and define explicit close/dispose semantics that stop the stream and cancel handlers. Because every consumer sees only the newest state, model one-shot effects (navigation, toasts) outside the state stream. Prefer the Cubit shape (public methods that call emit) for features where event traceability is not required, and graduate to full event-based Bloc only when onTransition logs earn their extra type weight.
code_sketch:
component Bloc:
    state: State = initial()          # single current state, immutable
    on(EventA) do a -> state = reduce(state, a); publish(state)
    on(EventB) do b -> state = reduce(state, b); publish(state)
    publish(s): for o in observers: o.onChange(previous, s)
                subscribers.push(s)   # hot stream, replays latest state
    close(): subscribers.close()      # late emissions must not reach views
pitfalls: Skipping the reducer and letting handlers mutate the state in place removes the traceability and equality guarantees the pattern exists for.
Pushing one-shot effects (navigation, toasts) through the state stream replays them to new subscribers and fires them after the screen is disposed.
Handlers are sequential by default; long-running handlers delay all later events unless an explicit concurrency policy is chosen.
Components and subscriptions that are never closed leak listeners and keep processing events for screens that no longer exist.
Emitting the same state value twice (equality-conflicting emission): Bloc skips the second emission silently, leaving the UI in an apparently broken state with no error message.
Async gaps without isClosed guards: an async handler that runs after the Bloc is disposed will throw StateError or crash; always check isClosed before emit in async handlers.
Using a plain Provider instead of BlocProvider to provide a Bloc: the lifecycle management (close on dispose) is bypassed, causing memory leaks.
Passing a Bloc instance to BlocProvider.create: the provider takes ownership and calls close(); if the caller also closes the bloc, a double-close error occurs.
Emitting from outside the component (a public mutable state field, or a handler that mutates the state object in place), which breaks immutability and traceability at once.

Blocs that know about other Blocs: direct Bloc-to-Bloc coupling creates tight sibling dependencies that are hard to maintain; coordinate via the widget layer (BlocListener adding events to another Bloc) or via shared repository streams instead.

Wrong move: wrapping every screen in a BLoC because the convention says so -> most app state (toggles, tabs, dropdowns, scroll positions) is not a state machine, so three files per boolean add ceremony with no traceability payoff -> reserve BLoC for state-machine-shaped flows (auth, checkout, payments) and use setState/ValueNotifier or a lighter provider for the rest.

Wrong move: defaulting to BLoC on a small CRUD app or prototype -> event/state types, stream plumbing and rebuild tuning cost days while nothing observable improves -> pick the simplest architecture that solves the actual problem and graduate only when a feature earns the structure.

Wrong move: letting app code depend on the bloc package's idioms everywhere -> major library upgrades ripple through all business logic (version churn is a documented ecosystem cost) -> keep core logic behind framework-agnostic repositories and use cases so only the presentation adapter imports bloc.
